Jonker2 1Department of Physics, University of Bath, Claverton Down, Bath BA2 7AY, UK 2Department of Astrophysics/IMAPP, Radboud University, 6525 AJ Nĳmegen, The Netherlands 3Department of Physics, University of Warwick, Gibbet Hill Road, Coventry, CV4 7AL, UK 4Oxford Theoretical Physics, Beecroft Building, Clarendon Laboratory, Parks Road, Oxford, OX1 3PU, United Kingdom Accepted 2025 October 07. Received 2025 September 17; in original form 2025 June 02 ABSTRACT The Luminous Fast Blue Optical Transient (LFBOT) AT 2018cow is the prototype of its class with an extensive set of multiwavelength observations. Despite a rich data set there is, still, no consensus about the physical nature and origin of this event. AT 2018cow remained UV bright 2–4 years after the explosion, which points at an additional energy injection source, most likely from an accretion disk. We present additional late time UV data obtained with the Hubble Space Telescope, to show there is no significant fading in the optical since the last epoch and only marginal fading in the UV. The new UV data points match the predictions of previously published accretion disk models, where the disk is assumed to form from the tidal disruption of a low mass star by an intermediate mass black hole. This consistency provides evidence that AT 2018cow could indeed be a tidal disruption event. The marginal decay is in contrast with the predictions of light curves produced by interacting supernovae. The difference between expectations for disc emission and interacting supernovae will further increase with time, making data at even later times a route to robustly rule out interaction between supernova ejecta and circumstellar material. Key words: stars: individual: AT 2018cow – ultraviolet: stars – supernovae: general – transients: supernovae – transients: tidal disruption events 1 INTRODUCTION Luminous fast blue optical transients (LFBOTs) are a relatively recently discovered class of multi wavelength transients (Prentice et al. 2018; Perley et al. 2019; Coppejans et al. 2020; Ho et al. 2020; Perley et al. 2021; Yao et al. 2022; Matthews et al. 2023; Chrimes et al. 2024; Ho et al. 2024; Pursiainen et al. 2025). These events are characterised by fast rise and decay times, high peak luminosities (absolute peak magnitude 𝑀≲−19), and early spectra dominated by a blue featureless continuum. There are currently less than ten LFBOTs known. The prototypical LFBOT is AT 2018cow (Prentice et al. 2018; Perley et al. 2019) which was detected and reported rapidly, and is the closest known LFBOT at a distance of just 63.0±4.4 Mpc (𝑧= 0.01404 ± 0.00002, SDSS DR6; AdelmanMcCarthy et al. 2008). This combination triggered an extensive, multiwavelength followup campaign, resulting in AT 2018cow being one of the most wellstudied transients to date. Other LBFOTs were either at greater (sometimes cosmological, 𝑧> 0.1) distances (e.g., AT2020mrf; Yao et al. 2022 and AT2023fhn; Chrimes et al. 2024) or were not immediately recognised as LFBOTs (e.g., CSS161010 which was reported in 2016,

resulting in AT 2018cow being one of the most wellstudied transients to date. Other LBFOTs were either at greater (sometimes cosmological, 𝑧> 0.1) distances (e.g., AT2020mrf; Yao et al. 2022 and AT2023fhn; Chrimes et al. 2024) or were not immediately recognised as LFBOTs (e.g., CSS161010 which was reported in 2016, but only published in 2020; Coppejans et al. 2020; Gutiérrez et al. 2024), meaning there was less opportunity to obtain such extensive data as exists for AT 2018cow. The ultimate physical origin of LFBOTs remains uncertain, despite much progress being made in the last few years. Among a wide ★Email: ai707@bath.ac.uk range of theoretical models seeking to explain the origin of these events, the community has converged onto a muchreduced subset of models: the ‘naked’ engine model, where the emission comes from accretion onto a compact object formed during a corecollapse supernova with small ejecta mass (e.g., Prentice et al. 2018; Perley et al. 2019; Margutti et al. 2019; Mohan et al. 2020), an intermediate mass black hole (IMBH) tidally disrupting a white dwarf (WD) (e.g., Kuin et al. 2019; Perley et al. 2019), or a lowmass main sequence star (Inkenhaag et al. 2023), the tidal disruption of a WolfRayet star by a stellar mass black hole (Metzger 2022), or interaction between an outflow and a dense circumstellar medium (e.g., Fox & Smith 2019; Leung et al. 2020; Xiang et al. 2021; Pellegrino et al. 2022). Both a compact object (e.g., Margutti et al. 2019; Pasham et al. 2021) and CSM (e.g., Coppejans et al. 2020) have been observationally shown to be present in these systems, providing observational justification to consider the models as well. Furthermore, (Gutiérrez et al. 2024) provide spectroscopic evidence in support of the TDE scenario for CSS161010. The model convergence to the aforementioned subset of models is due to both the discovery of more LFBOTs in recent years and early time observations across the electromagnetic spectrum, but specifically due to HST UV detections of the archetypal LFBOT AT 2018cow at late times (Sun et al. 2022, 2023; Chen et al. 2023; Inkenhaag et al. 2023), which ruled out many promising model candidates. These latetime HST detections demonstrated that the UV emission of AT 2018cow remained several magnitudes brighter at Δ𝑡∼700 −1450 days than the extrapolated early time emission (Sun et al. 2022), and varied only slowly in this phase (Sun et al. © 20252025 The Authors arXiv:2510.08505v1 [astroph.HE] 9 Oct 2025 2 A. (2022) argued this late time emission was likely not from accretion onto a compact object, arguing that the plateau phase in the light curve would require delayed accretion on the object, Inkenhaag et al. (2023) instead showed that the accretion disk formed at early times by a MBH = 103.2±0.8 M⊙black hole tidally disrupting a low mass star could, in fact, readily explain the observed late time properties, rejuvenating the tidal disruption event (TDE) model. MBH = 103.2±0.8 M⊙black hole tidally disrupting a low mass star could, in fact, readily explain the observed late time properties, rejuvenating the tidal disruption event (TDE) model. Indeed, bright longlived UV emission is a ubiquitous feature of tidal disruption events (Van Velzen et al. 2019; Mummery & Balbus 2020; Mummery et al. 2024b). Every classical (galactic centre supermassive black hole) TDE which is nearby (𝑧< 0.07) and has more than 3 years of optical/UV data has been detected to undergo this late time “plateau phase” in the UV (for a total of 𝑁= 40 sources) Mummery et al. (2024b); Mummery & van Velzen (2024). The amplitude of this plateau is known (theoretically and observationally) to correlate with the central black hole mass with a 𝐿plat ∝𝑀2/3 BH scaling (Mummery et al. 2024b). It is this scaling which, when applied to the low luminosity of AT 2018cow at late times, implies an intermediate mass black hole (Inkenhaag et al. 2023). In this work we present an additional set of multiwavelength observations of AT 2018cow at ∼1900 days, using HST/WFC3 in four filters. In Section 2 we describe the data and the analysis. We also present our results in this section. Section 3 contains the discussion of the results in the context of the progenitor models of AT 2018cow, and we summarise our findings and conclusion in Section 4. All magnitudes are presented in the AB magnitude system unless specified otherwise, with 1𝜎errors. Upper limits are defined as 3𝜎 upper limit. Throughout the paper we use H0 = 67.8 km s−1 Mpc−1, Ωm = 0.308 and ΩΛ = 0.692 (Planck Collaboration et al. 2016). 2 DATA AND ANALYSIS We present new HST data taken with the UltravioletVisible (UVIS) channel of the Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3) in four filters (proposal ID 17290, PI Y. Chen), two ultraviolet (UV) and two optical filters, corresponding to the filters usedfor theprevious datapresented in Sun et al. (2022, 2023); Chen et al. (2023) and Inkenhaag et al. (2023). The F225W, F336W and F555W data were taken 1900 days after the first detection of the transients, while the F814W observations failed at that epoch and so were repeated at 2043 days. We take the first detection of the transient as T0 = 58285.44 (Perley et al. 2019). All observations were completed using gyro guiding, after the reacquisition of the guide star failed. We provide a summary of the observations in Table 1. To obtain photometry of the new data, we follow the procedure described in Inkenhaag et al. (2023). In short, this entails combining the individual _flc images using astrodrizzle from the python package drizzlepack (Hoffmann et al. 2021)1. The final pixel scale is decreased to final_scale=0.025 for a better sampled point spread function (PSF). We then align the new images to the images in the same filter taken at 714 days from (Inkenhaag et al. 2023), as the 714 days images were aligned between the different filters and aligning to images in the same filter is more accurate. The images used in Inkenhaag et al. (2023) were

the new images to the images in the same filter taken at 714 days from (Inkenhaag et al. 2023), as the 714 days images were aligned between the different filters and aligning to images in the same filter is more accurate. The images used in Inkenhaag et al. (2023) were aligned at the pixel level, to allow for dual image mode aperture photometry. We perform aperture photometry on the images using Source Extractor (Bertin & Arnouts 1 https://drizzlepac.readthedocs.io/en/latest/ astrodrizzle.html 1996) in dual image mode. The base image used for source detected is the F336W image at 714 days, and the aperture used is 0.08 arcsec, which correspond to a diameter of ∼2 times the Full Width at Half Maximum (FWHM). Enclosed energy corrections are done using the table provided in the WFC3 handbook website2. As in Inkenhaag et al. (2023), we also perform PSF photometry using dolphot (v2.0; Dolphin 2000), which performs PSF photometry on the individual _flc frames and combines the individual measurements into a final (Vega) magnitude for each source. We again use the F336W epoch one image as our base image, align the individual _flc images to this image using tweakreg from drizzlepack, and use the sources detected in this base image as fixed positions in the “warmstart" option in dolphot for our new images. We use the zeropoints from the WFC3 instrument handbook3 to convert between Vega and AB magnitudes. The results of our aperture and PSF photometry are listed in Table 1 and we plot the lightcurve including the new data in Figure 1, using the previous data from Inkenhaag et al. (2023). There is significant fading between the last epoch previously reported in Inkenhaag et al. (2023) and the new data at 1900/2043 days only in the F336W filter. In none of the other filters do we detect evidence for fading at more than 3𝜎. 3 DISCUSSION As was also the case in Inkenhaag et al. (2023), the dolphot PSF photometric measurements are not fully consistent with the aperture photometry, especially in the optical bands, where dolphot gives fainter magnitudes than Source Extractor. This can be explained by an extended background source at the position of AT 2018cow, for which a circular aperture will naturally measure more flux than when fitting with a PSF. The presence of this underlying, extended source was shown to be likely in Inkenhaag et al. (2023), with its main contribution being in the optical bands. In the UV bands the difference in magnitude between aperture and PSF photometry is smaller. This is because there is still a point source present at the position of AT 2018cow, which dominates the flux. Therefore the ratio between the point source flux and the flux of the extended region is much higher, leading to a smaller difference when performing aperture photometry compared to PSF photometry. Despite the difference in magnitudes between the methods, when we compare the change in magnitude between epochs 3 and 4, both methods provide similar results. As can be seen from the lightcurves in Figure 1, the AT 2018cow UV plateau in the lightcurve of two UV bands is even clearer now than it was at 1474 days. This plateau behaviour is also seen in all (𝑁= 40) TDEs at 𝑧< 0.07 with more than three years of data available (Mummery et al. 2024b; Mummery & van Velzen 2024), including those TDEs around lower mass SMBHs (<106.5M⊙; Van Velzen et al. 2019; Mummery & van Velzen 2024). Additionally, and crucially, one can see from Figure 2 that the newest data points are entirely consistent with the predictions from the disk modelling presented in Inkenhaag et al. (2023). This model is premised upon an accretion disk that forms close to the black hole which then cools down and spreads out (to conserve angular momentum) when mass is accreted onto the compact object. There is no external source of material being added onto the accretion disk in this model and therefore it is not analogous to either an AGN disk or a highmass Xray binary disk, it has to be an isolated object spontaneously forming the accretion disk close to the black hole, which we believe is most likely to be a TDE4. To explore how the underlying cluster might influence the parameters of the disk model, we also run the disk model for the scenarios were we assume an average and a blue underlying stellar cluster and plot these in Figure 3. As can be seen from Table 2, the black hole mass shifts by ∼0.3 dex between the no underlying cluster and the average/blue underlying clusters scenarios. However, the uncertainty on the black hole mass is of the order of ∼0.5 dex, which means both scenarios are still consistent with the decay rate for a TDE disk model with a black hole mass which is consistent with that presented in Inkenhaag et al. (2023). While the disk model presented in Inkenhaag et al. (2023) (and reproduced here) assumed that the disk formed from the tidal disruption of a lowmass star, we stress that the latetime UV plateau luminosity is only a weak function of stellar properties (Mummery et al. 2024b), meaning that a white dwarf tidal disruption (which may well provide a natural explanation for the rapid early light curve decay) is also consistent with this late time UV emission, and would require only a slightly higher black hole mass than presented in Inkenhaag et al. (2023). If a much higher mass star was involved in the disruption (such as a WolfRayet star as has been suggested by Metzger 2022) then a less massive black hole would be required. Inkenhaag et al. (2025) investigated the possibility that the late time emission of AT 2018cow is from an interaction between SN ejecta and a (dense) CSM. There is a lack of modelling of SN lightcurves and spectra beyond ∼300 days in the UV for interacting SNe, and the available data for interacting SNe at the timescales of the latest observations of AT 2018cow are very limited (Inkenhaag et al. 2025). Khatami & Kasen (2024) model various configurations of CSM out to timescales similar to the observations of AT 2018cow, though clearly a special ejecta and CSM geometry is needed to produce a lightcurve that has a plateau phase at later times. In Figure 2 we have linearly extrapolated the synthetic photometry of two known interacting SNe out to later times. Comparing this to the model from Dessart et al. the synthetic photometry of two known interacting SNe out to later times. Comparing this to the model from Dessart et al. (2023) of a 15.2 M⊙red super giant exploding with injected energy, representing the interaction with the CSM, we can see that observations and modelling yield a range of decay rates for CSM interaction. Despite variation in these decay rates, the lightcurve decay in interacting SNe is generally much faster (and they typically are much fainter at Δ𝑡∼2000 days) than the predictions for the TDE disk model, even when subtracting a blue underlying source, adding to the evidence for a TDE nature of AT 2018cow. We can also see from Figure 2 the variety in magnitudes from observations and modelling for CSM interaction. The late time UV observations of AT 2018cow are consistent in magnitude with the upper range of these magnitudes. At even later times, out to ∼3000 days, we see a significant difference in magnitude between emission from even the brightest SN–CSM interactions and an accretion disk from a TDE. We will therefore need (at least) another observation on this time scale to fully distinguish between the models. 4 SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION We present a new epoch of latetime HST observations of AT 2018cow. There is significant fading since the last epoch only in the F336W filter, while fading in the F225W, F555W and F814W filters is marginal. The fading in UV between the previous epoch and the epoch presented in this paper is consistent with the fading predicted by the TDE disk model presented in Inkenhaag et al. (2023) (and the BH mass is consistent with previous modelling when including this latest datapoint) and is significantly slower than observed in interacting SNe. The limited available simulations of the UV brightness of interacting CCSNe, which we need to extrapolate to the times observed in this work, also fade faster than what we observe for AT 2018cow. However, purely based on brightness, we cannot rule out CSM interaction just yet, especially if we assume a blue underlying star cluster. Nevertheless, we conclude that the late time UV emission of AT 2018cow is an argument for a TDE nature of this event, supported by the latest epoch being consistent with model predictions. A final data point when TDE and CSMinteraction models and observations have diverged significantly, around 2800–3000 days, is needed to fully rule out (on brightness arguments) SN–CSM interaction as the nature of the latetime emission.
